fuentes/tabla-claudiana/titulo.texto: Claudian Tablet (Claudius's speech on the Gaulish notables)

fuentes/tabla-claudiana/soporte.texto: Bronze plaque found in 1528 at the Croix-Rousse in Lyon (Lugdunum, Gallo-Roman Museum)

fuentes/tabla-claudiana/resumen.texto: Part of the speech that Emperor Claudius delivered in the Senate in 48 so that the notables of Gallia Comata could become senators, engraved in bronze by the Gaulish cities and displayed in the federal sanctuary of Lugdunum. Claudius recalls that Rome had always incorporated foreigners, from the Etruscan kings to the senators of Vienne, and that Gaul, after ten years of war with Caesar, had given a hundred years of loyalty. The lower part of two columns survives.

fuentes/tabla-claudiana/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the few speeches by a Roman emperor preserved in his own words, and it allows comparison with the version Tacitus wrote in the Annals (XI.23-25), shorter and more elegant: a case study in how ancient historians rewrote speeches. It is also a key document on the integration of the Gaulish aristocracies into the Empire.

fuentes/tabla-claudiana/leer.0.titulo.texto: Latin text and French translation on Wikisource

fuentes/inscripciones-galogriegas/titulo.texto: Gaulish inscriptions in the Greek alphabet

fuentes/inscripciones-galogriegas/autor.texto: Gauls of Narbonensis and the Rhône valley

fuentes/inscripciones-galogriegas/soport.texto: Stone, ceramic vessels and metal objects

fuentes/inscripciones-galogriegas/resume.texto: About three hundred inscriptions, mostly from the lower Rhône valley (Nîmes, Glanum, Vaison, Cavaillon), in which the Gauls wrote their language in the Greek alphabet learned from Massalia, from the 3rd or 2nd century BC to the beginning of the Roman period: dedications to gods, epitaphs, owners' names on vessels. They were collected by Michel Lejeune in the first volume of the Recueil des inscriptions gauloises (1985). They confirm what Caesar says: that the Helvetii kept their censuses and the Druids their public and private accounts “in Greek letters” (BG I.29, VI.14).

fuentes/inscripciones-galogriegas/por_qu.texto: They are proof that the Gauls wrote before the conquest, against the idea of a purely oral culture; at the same time, their number is small and their texts brief, which shows a limited use of writing. Together with coins, they give the names of people and gods in the form the Gauls wrote them.

fuentes/inscripciones-galogriegas/leer.0.texto: Recueil informatisé des inscriptions gauloises (RIIG), database of Gaulish inscriptions

fuentes/cuentas-de-la-graufesenque/resum.texto: Dozens of plates on which the potters of the great sigillata workshop at La Graufesenque noted, before each collective firing, the name of each craftsman, the type of vessel and the quantity, in a kiln that could fire tens of thousands of pieces. Most are in Gaulish, with words such as “tuθos” (firing), the ordinals from “cintux” (first) to “decametos” (tenth), and Celtic and Latin names mixed together. They were published by Robert Marichal in 1988.

fuentes/cuentas-de-la-graufesenque/por_q.texto: It is the largest body of Gaulish texts and shows that in the 1st century Gaulish was written in everyday life and at work, in an industrial centre that exported to the whole Empire. It is a unique source for the organization of craft labor and for Gaulish–Latin bilingualism.

fuentes/teja-de-chateaubleau/resumen.texto: Tile found in 1997 at the Gallo-Roman sanctuary of Châteaubleau (Seine-et-Marne), with an eleven-line text in Gaulish, one of the longest in Latin cursive along with the Larzac and Chamalières tablets, from the late Roman period (2nd to 4th centuries, according to the authors). Its interpretation is difficult: most of those who studied it, such as Pierre-Yves Lambert, Wolfgang Meid and David Stifter, read it as a kind of marriage proposal, and Bernard Mees as a curse.

fuentes/teja-de-chateaubleau/por_que_imp.texto: It shows that Gaulish continued to be written, and probably spoken, in the Paris region in the Roman period, and it provides vocabulary and grammar not known from other texts. The divergent readings are an example of how little of the language is still understood.

fuentes/monedas-galas/resumen.texto: The Gauls minted coins from the 3rd century BC, first imitating the gold stater of Philip II of Macedon, which mercenaries brought, and then with their own designs that became increasingly abstract; in the 2nd century BC central-eastern Gaul adopted a silver standard compatible with the Roman denarius. From the late 2nd century BC many carry legends in Greek or Latin letters with the names of peoples and chieftains: VERCINGETORIXS on Arvernian staters, DVBNOREIX among the Aedui, ORCITIRIX, COMMIOS, and those of chiefs whom Caesar does not name.

fuentes/monedas-galas/por_que_importa.texto: They are documents written by the Gauls themselves, showing a monetary economy, contacts with the Mediterranean and the existence of powers that minted coins; the names allow Caesar to be checked against an independent source. It is debated whether the heads are portraits (the Vercingetorix head is generally considered an Apollo) and whether the names are always those of the known chiefs or homonyms.

fuentes/bilingue-de-vercelli/resumen.texto: Inscription found in 1960 in Vercelli that marks the boundary of a field which Acisius Argantocomaterego left “in common for the gods and men”, with the Latin text and a version in Cisalpine Gaulish written in the North Etruscan alphabet of the Lepontii (“akisios arkatokokmaterekos tośokote atoś teuoxtonion eu”). It dates from the 1st century BC, when Transpadane Gaul was passing to Roman citizenship.

fuentes/bilingue-de-vercelli/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of the few Gaulish–Latin bilingual inscriptions, key to understanding Gaulish vocabulary (“teuoxtonion”, gods and men) and the coexistence of the two languages in Cisalpine Gaul before Latin prevailed.

fuentes/fusayolas-galas/resumen.texto: A group of spindle whorls (weights for spinning), found mostly at Autun and Sens, with brief phrases in Gaulish, in Latin or in a mixture of the two, such as “nata uimpi curmi da” (“pretty girl, give me beer”) or “moni gnatha gabi buððutton imon”, which is translated as “my girl, take my…”, with a last word that some understand as “little kiss” and others with a sexual meaning. They are generally dated to the 3rd and 4th centuries, and all translations are tentative.

fuentes/fusayolas-galas/por_que_importa.texto: They are among the latest surviving Gaulish texts and show a language still alive in everyday life and mixed with Latin. The most common reading is that they were courtship gifts from suitors to girls; others see double-entendre jokes or good-luck formulas. They are also a rare witness to women and the work of spinning.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-alisiia/soporte.texto: Stone slab found in 1839 at Alise-Sainte-Reine

fuentes/inscripcion-de-alisiia/resumen.texto: Inscription in Gaulish stating that Martial, son of Dannotalo, dedicated a building to the god Ucuetis together with the smiths who honor him “at Alisiia”. It dates from the 1st century, in the Roman period.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-alisiia/por_que_i.texto: It is the main epigraphic argument for placing Caesar's Alesia on Mont Auxois, together with the excavations, and it shows that metalworkers had their own cult there. The dedication is religious; its importance here is as a witness to the name of the place and to the language.

fuentes/dialogos-sulpicio-severo/titulo.texto: Dialogues on the Virtues of Martin

fuentes/dialogos-sulpicio-severo/resumen.texto: Dialogues in which Sulpicius Severus and his friends speak of the monks of Egypt and the miracles of Martin of Tours. In one of them (I.27) a Gallic interlocutor apologizes for his rustic Latin, and another replies that he should speak “in Celtic or, if you prefer, in Gaulish”, provided he speaks of Martin.

fuentes/dialogos-sulpicio-severo/por_que.texto: The passage is one of the most cited testimonies that Gaulish was still spoken in Gaul around 404. Some specialists read it literally and others as a rhetorical joke about provincial Latin, so it is not enough on its own to prove that the language remained alive.

fuentes/contra-las-herejias-ireneo/resum.texto: Treatise in five books against the Gnostics, written in Lugdunum around 180, which sets out the faith of the Church based on the tradition of the apostles. In the preface, Irenaeus apologizes for his style because he lives “among the Celts” and most of the time speaks “a barbarian tongue”.

fuentes/contra-las-herejias-ireneo/por_q.texto: It is a fundamental work of Christian theology and, incidentally, one of the earliest testimonies that Gaulish was spoken in the capital of the Three Gauls at the end of the 2nd century.

fuentes/contra-las-herejias-ireneo/leer..texto: Book I in the English translation of the Ante-Nicene Fathers (Wikisource)

fuentes/becoming-roman-woolf/titulo.texto: Becoming Roman: The Origins of Provincial Civilization in Gaul

fuentes/becoming-roman-woolf/resumen.texto: Woolf studies Gaul between the conquest and the 3rd century as a process in which the Gallic elites actively adopted Roman ways of life (cities, wine, houses, epigraphy, names) out of their own interest, while “Roman culture” itself changed. He rejects both the idea of Romanization imposed from above and that of a hidden Celtic resistance.

fuentes/becoming-roman-woolf/por_que_imp.texto: It is the standard work on Roman Gaul in English and the one that redirected the debate on “Romanization”. Jane Webster and David Mattingly, among others, criticized it for concentrating on the elites and leaving aside peasants, slaves and forms of mixing or resistance (“creolization”, “discrepant experiences”).

fuentes/he-came-he-saw-we-counted-henige.texto: He came, he saw, we counted: the historiography and demography of Caesar's Gallic numbers
Article in Annales de démographie historique (1998, no. 1, pp. 215-242)

Henige examines the figures in the Commentaries and the totals of dead and enslaved given by Plutarch and Pliny, and how modern historians, from the 19th century on, repeated or adjusted them without any independent basis. He argues that Caesar subordinated accuracy to effect and that his numbers serve to reveal his propaganda, not the demography of Gaul.

It is the standard study of the critique of Caesar's figures and is cited throughout the debate on the demography of the conquest and on “genocide”. Its skepticism does not deny that mortality and enslavement were massive: what it disputes is that they can be measured with Caesar's numbers.

fuentes/rambaud-deformacion-historica-ce.texto: The art of historical distortion in Caesar's Commentaries

Rambaud analyzes the Commentaries as a work of propaganda built with subtle techniques: omissions, changes of order, attribution of failures to subordinates, speeches put in the mouths of enemies, and an impersonal third-person style that gives an appearance of objectivity.

It was the book that established a critical reading of Caesar in modern historiography. It was criticized for attributing deliberate intent to every silence or inaccuracy; later works, such as those gathered by Kathryn Welch and Anton Powell in Julius Caesar as Artful Reporter (1998), keep the idea of a Caesar who writes for his career but qualify its scope.

fuentes/cesar-y-el-genocidio-raaflaub/ti.texto: Caesar and Genocide: Confronting the Dark Side of Caesar's Gallic Wars

fuentes/cesar-y-el-genocidio-raaflaub/so.texto: Article in New England Classical Journal 48.1 (2021), pp. 54-80

fuentes/cesar-y-el-genocidio-raaflaub/re.texto: Raaflaub examines the episodes in which Caesar says he exterminated or sold entire peoples (the massacre of the Usipetes and Tencteri, which he calls Caesar's worst atrocity in Gaul; the Eburones; the Atuatuci; Avaricum), and asks whether they fit the modern definition of genocide and whether it is fair to judge Caesar by a norm formulated in the 20th century. Without justifying them, he places these actions within the customs of ancient and Roman imperial warfare and contrasts the brutal conqueror with the victor who displayed clemency; he concludes that several cases fit the definition. He recalls that in Rome what shocked people about the massacre of 55 BC was the violation of a truce, which led Cato to propose handing Caesar over to the enemy, and that the population of Gaul cannot be calculated with certainty: the reasonable modern estimates, according to Wolfgang Will (1992), reach 8, 10 or 12 million.

fuentes/cesar-y-el-genocidio-raaflaub/po.texto: It is one of the most cited debates on the use of the term “genocide” for the conquest of Gaul. The main objections, which the article itself discusses, are that applying a legal category of the 20th century to antiquity is anachronistic, and that the figures on which the horror rests are Caesar's and cannot be verified.

fuentes/cesar-y-el-genocidio-raaflaub/le.texto: Article with its PDF in the open-access repository where the journal is published (College of the Holy Cross)

fuentes/conquista-y-violencia-masiva-roy.texto: Conquest, mass violence and ethnic stereotyping: investigating Caesar's actions in the Germanic frontier zone
Article in Journal of Roman Archaeology

Roymans combines the Commentaries with the archaeology of the lower Rhine and the Meuse: he identifies at Kessel the site of the massacre of the Usipetes and Tencteri (55 BC) and links a fall in the population visible in the settlements to the campaigns against the Eburones. He argues that Caesar applied mass violence, in some cases genocidal, against the peoples he presented as “Germanic”.

It is the most systematic attempt to check archaeologically the most violent episodes of the conquest. Roymans does not argue for total extermination: in a work with Manuel Fernández-Götz (2019) he explains the disappearance of the Eburones from the later political map by a sharp population decline, a partial genocide, and not by the death of all of them. Attributing the remains at Kessel to that specific episode, and reading the population decline as a direct effect of the war, remain hypotheses, which depend in part on Caesar's own account.

fuentes/la-ville-celtique-fichtl/titulo.texto: The Celtic city: the oppida from 150 BC to AD 15

fuentes/la-ville-celtique-fichtl/resumen.texto: Synthesis of the Celtic oppida of Europe, which Fichtl presents as true cities: capitals of Gallic “city-states”, often founded all at once by political decision, with walls, craft quarters, public spaces and sanctuaries.

fuentes/la-ville-celtique-fichtl/por_que.texto: It is a reference for understanding the urbanization of Gaul before Rome, against the image of the barbarian without cities. Other archaeologists, such as John Collis, question the use of the word “city” and point out that many oppida were sparsely populated.

fuentes/los-origenes-de-bretana-fleuriot.texto: The origins of Brittany: the emigration

Fleuriot studies the emigration of Britons to Armorica between the 4th and 6th centuries and argues that Breton is not merely Brittonic transplanted: in Armorica a spoken Gaulish would have survived and influenced it, above all in the dialect of Vannes.

It is the basis of the thesis of a continuity of Gaulish in Brittany, which takes up François Falc'hun's view of the Vannes dialect. Kenneth Jackson (A Historical Phonology of Breton, 1967) had held that Breton derives only from Brittonic; the main criticism of Fleuriot is that there is little indisputable evidence that Gaulish survived so late precisely in Armorica (the signs of a late Gaulish are stronger for central Gaul and the Alps), so the Gaulish substratum of Breton remains a hypothesis.

fuentes/vino-italiano-en-la-galia-tchern.texto: Italian wine in Gaul at the end of the Republic
Chapter in Trade in the Ancient Economy (Garnsey, Hopkins and Whittaker, eds.)

Tchernia studies the distribution of Dressel 1 amphorae of Italian wine in Gaul, calculates the volume of that trade and links it to Diodorus's phrase about the amphora exchanged for a slave: wine would have paid for the slave labor of Italy.

It set the model of “wine for slaves” used to explain the economy of Gaul before Caesar. Matthieu Poux (2004) and others stressed the social and ritual use of wine among the Gallic elites and warned that Diodorus's phrase is also a commonplace about the drunken barbarian.

fuentes/the-beginnings-of-rome-cornell/r.texto: History of Rome from the Bronze Age to the Punic Wars, which combines the literary tradition with archaeology; on the Gallic sack, he argues that it was a real event but that archaeology shows no general destruction, and that many details in Livy are later elaborations.

fuentes/the-beginnings-of-rome-cornell/p.texto: It is the standard synthesis on early Rome. More skeptical authors, such as Gary Forsythe (A Critical History of Early Rome, 2005), criticize it for relying too heavily on the historical core of the literary tradition.

fuentes/the-revolt-of-vindex-brunt/titul.texto: The Revolt of Vindex and the Fall of Nero

fuentes/the-revolt-of-vindex-brunt/resum.texto: Brunt argues that Vindex's revolt was not a national Gallic uprising against Rome but a revolt by a senator against Nero, supported by part of the Gallo-Roman aristocracy, and that its defeat was due to the Rhine legions seeing it as a Gallic threat.

fuentes/the-revolt-of-vindex-brunt/por_q.texto: It changed the interpretation of the revolt, which 19th-century historiography read in nationalist terms, and it remains the starting point of the debate.

fuentes/peasant-revolts-thompson/titulo.texto: Peasant revolts in late Roman Gaul and Spain

fuentes/peasant-revolts-thompson/resumen.texto: Thompson interprets the Bagaudae revolts as uprisings of peasants and tenant farmers against landowners and the Roman fisc, which came to create independent zones in Armorica and in the Ebro valley.

fuentes/peasant-revolts-thompson/por_que.texto: It is the classic, Marxist-inspired reading of the Bagaudae. John Drinkwater and others discussed it and proposed seeing them as regional self-defense groups led by local notables in the vacuum of imperial power.

personas/ambigato/resumen.texto: King of the Bituriges who, according to Livy (V.34), in the time of Tarquinius Priscus sent his nephews Belovesus and Segovesus to look for land because Gaul was overpopulated. He appears only in Livy and is almost certainly a legendary figure: the account explains by a king-led migration what archaeology shows as a gradual arrival.

personas/beloveso/resumen.texto: Nephew of Ambigatus who, according to Livy (V.34), crossed the Alps with the Bituriges, Arverni, Senones, Aedui, Ambarri, Carnutes and Aulerci, defeated the Etruscans near the Ticino and founded Mediolanum (Milan). Livy places him around 600 BC, two centuries before Polybius and archaeology place the great Gallic entry into the Po valley; most historians consider him a legend of origin.

personas/segoveso/resumen.texto: Brother of Belovesus, to whom, according to Livy (V.34), the omens assigned the Hercynian Forest in central Europe. He is a legendary figure who appears only in that passage.

personas/breno/resumen.texto: Chief of the Senones who, according to the Roman tradition, defeated the Romans at the Allia and sacked Rome around 390 BC (Varro's date; Polybius gives 387-386). Livy (V.48) attributes to him the phrase “vae victis” (“woe to the vanquished!”) when he threw his sword onto the scales of the ransom, and Plutarch (Camillus 28) repeats the scene. Polybius (II.18) does not name him; many historians think “Brennus” may be a title or a name taken from the Brennus who attacked Delphi in 279 BC, and that the anecdote is a later Roman elaboration.

personas/marco-furio-camilo/resumen.texto: Roman general who took Veii (396 BC) and who, according to Livy (V.46-49) and Plutarch (Camillus), returned from exile as dictator, stopped the payment of the ransom to the Gauls and defeated them. Polybius (II.18, II.22) does not name him: he says that the Gauls made a pact, returned the city and went back unbeaten with their booty because the Veneti were invading their lands; Diodorus (XIV.116-117) says they took the gold and that Camillus later defeated them, when they were besieging Veascium, and recovered it, and Strabo (V.2.3) attributes that victory to the people of Caere. For this reason his arrival at the moment of payment is considered a patriotic account that washed away Rome's humiliation. Livy (V.49) calls him the “second founder” of the city.

personas/marco-manlio-capitolino/resumen.texto: Consul in 392 BC who, according to Livy (V.47), defended the Capitol from a night assault by the Gauls, alerted by the sacred geese of Juno. Years later he was accused of aspiring to kingship and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock (Livy VI.20). The cognomen “Capitolinus” probably came from his house on the Capitol, and the story of the geese may have arisen to explain it.

personas/tito-manlio-torcuato/resumen.texto: Roman who, according to Livy (VII.9-10), following the annalist Claudius Quadrigarius (cited by Aulus Gellius, IX.13), killed in single combat a giant Gaul by the bridge over the Anio in 361 BC and took his torque, from which his family's cognomen came. He was three times consul and dictator; tradition also remembers him for having his own son executed for disobeying an order (340 BC).

personas/marco-valerio-corvo/resumen.texto: Roman who, according to Livy (VII.26), defeated a Gaul in single combat in 349 BC with the help of a crow that attacked the face of the enemy, which is said to be the origin of his cognomen. He was consul six times; tradition says he lived to a hundred. The duel, like Torquatus's, is an exemplary story of the Roman annalists.

personas/publio-decio-mus/resumen.texto: Roman consul who, according to Livy (X.28-29), consecrated himself to the gods of the dead (“devotio”) and charged the Gallic Senones at Sentinum (295 BC) to secure victory for his army, as his father had done in 340 BC. The repetition of the same gesture across three generations of Decii makes historians doubt the details.

personas/aneroesto/resumen.texto: King of the Gesatae, warriors from beyond the Alps whom the Insubres and Boii hired to invade Italy in 225 BC. According to Polybius (II.22-31), after the defeat at Telamon he fled with some companions and killed himself with them. We know him only from Polybius.

personas/concolitano/resumen.texto: King of the Gesatae together with Aneroestus in the invasion of 225 BC; Polybius (II.31) tells that he was captured at Telamon. What became of him is not known.

personas/viridomaro/resumen.texto: Chief of the Gesatae (or of the Insubres) killed in single combat by the consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus at Clastidium in 222 BC. Marcellus dedicated his arms to Jupiter Feretrius as “spolia opima”, the third and last time this was done in Rome (Plutarch, Marcellus 6-8, who calls him Britomartus). Propertius (IV.10) says that he boasted of descent from the Rhine.

personas/marco-claudio-marcelo/resumen.texto: Roman general who in 222 BC defeated the Insubres and Gesatae at Clastidium, killed their king Viridomarus with his own hand and offered his arms as “spolia opima” (Plutarch, Marcellus 6-8). He later fought Hannibal and took Syracuse (212 BC), where Archimedes died. He died in a Carthaginian ambush.

personas/cayo-flaminio/resumen.texto: Tribune of the plebs who in 232 BC had the “ager Gallicus”, taken from the Senones, distributed among citizens, a measure that Polybius (II.21) identifies as the cause of the great Gallic invasion of 225. As consul he crossed the Po and defeated the Insubres (223 BC), built the Via Flaminia and died at the battle of Lake Trasimene against Hannibal, at the hands of the Insubrian horseman Ducarius according to Livy (XXII.6).

personas/anibal/resumen.texto: Carthaginian general who in 218 BC crossed the Pyrenees, Gaul and the Alps to invade Italy. Polybius (III.34, III.60-74) and Livy (XXI-XXII) tell that he sought the alliance of the Boii and the Insubres, who had just been defeated by Rome, and that the Gauls formed a large part of his army at the Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae. Roman sources portray him as cruel and treacherous; Polybius, who spoke with witnesses, is more measured.

personas/ducario/resumen.texto: Insubrian horseman in Hannibal's army who, according to Livy (XXII.6), recognized the consul Gaius Flaminius at the battle of Lake Trasimene (217 BC) and killed him to avenge his people, who had been defeated by him six years earlier. He appears only in Livy.

personas/catumando/resumen.texto: Chieftain of the neighboring peoples of Massalia who, according to Justin (XLIII.5), besieged the city around 390 BC and lifted the siege after dreaming of a goddess whom the Massaliots identified with Minerva. The account, which comes from the Gallic historian Pompeius Trogus, synchronizes the episode with the sack of Rome; it is known only from Justin.

personas/luernio/resumen.texto: King of the Arverni, father of Bituitus, known from an account by Posidonius preserved by Athenaeus (IV.37): to win over the people he threw gold and silver coins from his chariot and offered a banquet in an enclosure twelve stadia on each side, with vats of drink. Strabo (IV.2.3) mentions him as an example of the wealth of the Arverni. He is the first figure of the Arvernian hegemony that Posidonius and Strabo describe; the banquet scene follows the Greek commonplace of the generous barbarian chief.

personas/bituito/resumen.texto: King of the Arverni, son of Luernius, who in 121 BC supported the Allobroges against Rome. Appian (Celtica 12) tells that he sent an embassy with dogs and a bard, and Florus (I.37) that he fought in silver armor on a chariot; he was defeated by Quintus Fabius Maximus near the Isère and later captured by treachery by Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, who sent him to Rome. He ended up confined at Alba Fucens (Valerius Maximus IX.6.3; Livy, Periocha 61).

personas/cneo-domicio-ahenobarbo/resumen.texto: Roman consul who in 121 BC defeated the Allobroges at Vindalium and captured the Arvernian king Bituitus by deception (Valerius Maximus IX.6.3). He toured the region riding an elephant (Suetonius, Nero 2) and gave his name to the Via Domitia, which linked Italy with Hispania through southern Gaul. He is the central figure in the creation of the province later called Narbonensis.

personas/quinto-fabio-maximo-alobrogico/.texto: Confluence of the Isère and the Rhône

Consul who in 121 BC defeated the Allobroges and the Arverni of Bituitus at the confluence of the Rhône and the Isère, and for this took the cognomen “Allobrogicus”. The epitomes of Livy and Orosius give figures of more than a hundred thousand Gallic dead that cannot be verified.

personas/catugnato/resumen.texto: Chief of the Allobroges who in 62-61 BC led a revolt against the Roman province, indebted and pressed by tax collectors; he was defeated by the governor Gaius Pomptinus (Cassius Dio XXXVII.47-48). How he ended is not known.

personas/cayo-mario/resumen.texto: Roman general of equestrian origin, seven times consul, who defeated the Teutones and Ambrones at Aquae Sextiae (102 BC) and the Cimbri at Vercellae (101 BC), according to Plutarch (Marius 15-27). Tradition credits him with reforming the army into professional legions, although historians debate how much he changed and how much came from earlier times. He later led the civil war against Sulla.

personas/boiorix/resumen.texto: King of the Cimbri. Livy's Periocha 67 presents him as the young man who killed the Roman legate Marcus Aurelius Scaurus, a prisoner of the Cimbri; according to Plutarch (Marius 25) he challenged Marius to fix the place and day of battle, and according to Orosius (V.16) he died fighting at Vercellae (101 BC). His name (“king of the Boii” or “king who strikes”) is Celtic, one of the arguments in the debate over whether the Cimbri were Celts or Germans.

personas/teutobodo/resumen.texto: King of the Teutones captured after the battle of Aquae Sextiae (102 BC) and paraded in Marius's triumph. Florus (I.38) says that he leaped over four or six horses; his figure is known only from late Roman authors.

personas/quinto-servilio-cepion/resumen.texto: Roman consul who in 106 BC took Tolosa and seized its sacred treasure, the “gold of Tolosa”, which disappeared on the road to Massalia. In 105 BC he refused to coordinate with the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus, and both armies were destroyed by the Cimbri at Arausio. He was condemned and died in exile at Smyrna.

personas/orgetorix/resumen.texto: The richest noble of the Helvetii according to Caesar (BG I.2-4), who in 61 BC persuaded his people to emigrate and secretly made a pact with Casticus and Dumnorix that the three would become kings. When discovered, he appeared for trial with ten thousand dependents and debtors and died before the verdict, perhaps by suicide. We know him only from Caesar, who presents him as the cause of the war; coins with the legend ORCITIRIX, from the area of the Aedui or the Sequani, might bear his name.

personas/casticus/resumen.texto: Sequanian noble, son of Catamantaloedes, a former king “friend of the Roman people”, with whom Orgetorix made a pact in 61 BC that he would seize the kingship of their people (Caesar, BG I.3). Nothing more is known about him.

personas/dumnorix/resumen.texto: Aeduan noble, brother of the druid Diviciacus, who grew rich by leasing tolls and had his own cavalry; he married the daughter of Orgetorix and helped the Helvetii in 58 BC (Caesar, BG I.3, I.9, I.18). In 54 BC he refused to embark for Britain with Caesar, fled, and was killed by the horsemen sent after him, crying out that he was “a free man of a free people” (BG V.6-7). Aeduan coins with the legend DVBNOREIX are often attributed to him.

personas/diviciaco/resumen.texto: Aeduan noble, brother of Dumnorix, who around 61 BC went to Rome to ask for help against Ariovistus and spoke before the Senate; Cicero, who hosted him, says in On Divination (I.90) that he was a druid and knew nature. He was Caesar's main Gallic ally in 58-57 BC (BG I.16-20, II.5-14), interceded for his brother and for the Bellovaci, and then disappears from the sources. He is the only druid of independent Gaul whose name we know from a contemporary.

personas/divico/resumen.texto: Chief of the Tigurini, one of the cantons of the Helvetii, who in 107 BC defeated and killed the consul Lucius Cassius Longinus; almost fifty years later he led the Helvetian embassy to Caesar (BG I.13-14), which puts a proud threat in his mouth. Only Caesar asserts that the two Divici were the same person.

personas/ariovisto/resumen.texto: German king of the Suebi who, called in by the Sequani and the Arverni against the Aedui around 71 BC, crossed the Rhine, defeated the Aedui at Magetobriga and took a third of Sequanian territory (Caesar, BG I.31). The Senate recognized him as “king and friend” in 59 BC, during Caesar's consulship, but in 58 BC Caesar defeated him in Alsace; he fled across the Rhine, and in the battle his two wives died, one Suebian and one Noric (BG I.53). By 54 BC he was already dead (BG V.29).

personas/galba-de-los-suesiones/resumen.texto: King of the Suessiones, chosen as leader of the Belgic coalition against Caesar in 57 BC (Caesar, BG II.4), when, according to the Remi informants, the Belgae promised nearly three hundred thousand warriors. After the defeat at the Axona he surrendered at Noviodunum and gave his sons as hostages (BG II.13).

personas/boduognato/resumen.texto: Chief of the Nervii who in 57 BC made a surprise attack on Caesar's legions by the river Sabis and came close to defeating them (Caesar, BG II.23). How he ended is not known; Caesar says that his people were almost annihilated, although three years later the Nervii were fighting again.

personas/viridovix/resumen.texto: Chief of the Unelli, in present-day Normandy, who in 56 BC gathered several coastal peoples and was defeated by the legate Quintus Titurius Sabinus with a feigned retreat (Caesar, BG III.17-19).

personas/adiatuano/resumen.texto: King of the Sotiates, in Aquitaine, who in 56 BC resisted the siege by Publius Crassus and tried a sortie with six hundred “soldurii”, warriors who according to Caesar (BG III.22) swore not to survive their chief. He surrendered and was pardoned. A coin with the legend REX ADIETVANVS might be his.

personas/comio/resumen.texto: Atrebatan whom Caesar made king of his people and sent to Britain as envoy in 55 BC (BG IV.21). In 52 BC he went over to the revolt and was one of the four leaders of the relief army at Alesia (BG VII.76); he survived an assassination attempt by the legate Volusenus (Hirtius, BG VIII.23), and at the end of 51 BC he submitted to Mark Antony on condition that he never again see a Roman (VIII.48). Frontinus (Stratagems II.13.11) says that he fled to Britain, where coins bearing his name (COMMIOS) appear, along with those of people said to be his sons, Tincomarus, Epillus and Verica.

personas/indutiomaro/resumen.texto: Noble of the Treveri, rival of his son-in-law Cingetorix for power, who rebelled against Caesar in 54 BC, attacked Labienus's camp and died in a sortie by Roman cavalry, which had orders to kill him before anyone else (Caesar, BG V.3-4, V.55-58).

personas/cingetorix/resumen.texto: Noble of the Treveri and ally of Caesar, whom Caesar installed as leader of his people against his father-in-law Indutiomarus (Caesar, BG V.3-4, VI.8). He is an example of how Caesar used the internal rivalries of the Gauls.

personas/ambiorix/resumen.texto: King of the Eburones, together with Catuvolcus, who in the winter of 54 BC deceived the legates Sabinus and Cotta into leaving their camp at Atuatuca and destroyed a legion and five cohorts, the worst defeat of Caesar in Gaul (BG V.26-37). He then besieged the camp of Quintus Cicero with the Nervii. Caesar ravaged the land of the Eburones for three years to trap him (BG VI.29-43; Hirtius VIII.24-25), but never succeeded and Ambiorix disappears from the sources. In the 19th century Belgium made him a national hero.

personas/catuvolco/resumen.texto: King of half of the Eburones, together with Ambiorix, in the revolt of 54 BC. Caesar (BG VI.31) tells that in 53 BC, old and too weak to flee, he poisoned himself with yew after cursing Ambiorix.

personas/acco/resumen.texto: Chief of the Senones who in 53 BC promoted a conspiracy against Caesar. Caesar tried him at an assembly of Gaul at Durocortorum (Reims) and had him executed “according to the custom of the ancestors”, flogged and beheaded (BG VI.44). His death was one of the motives for the general revolt of 52 BC (BG VII.1).

personas/tasgecio/resumen.texto: Noble of the Carnutes whom Caesar restored to the kingdom of his ancestors for services rendered; in the third year of his reign (54 BC) his political enemies murdered him (Caesar, BG V.25).

personas/cavarino/resumen.texto: Noble whom Caesar made king of the Senones; his people tried to kill him and expelled him in 54 BC (Caesar, BG V.54), and in 53 BC he accompanied Caesar with the Senonian cavalry (VI.5).

personas/vercingetorix/resumen.texto: Arvernian noble, son of Celtillus, who in 52 BC was expelled from Gergovia by his uncle Gobannitio, gathered an army, proclaimed himself king and led the greatest revolt against Caesar (BG VII.4). He applied a scorched-earth tactic, defeated Caesar at Gergovia and was confirmed as leader of all Gaul at Bibracte, but he was besieged at Alesia and surrendered (BG VII.89). He was displayed in Caesar's triumph of 46 BC and executed (Cassius Dio XL.41, XLIII.19). Almost everything we know comes from Caesar, who presents him as a worthy adversary to magnify his victory; since the 19th century he has been a national symbol of France. Gold coins with the legend VERCINGETORIXS confirm his name, although it is not known whether the head is a portrait.

personas/celtilo/resumen.texto: Arvernian noble, father of Vercingetorix, who according to Caesar (BG VII.4) held the leadership of all Gaul and was killed by his own people because he aspired to be king.

personas/litavico/resumen.texto: Aeduan noble who in 52 BC, at the head of ten thousand men sent to Caesar, convinced them with a false story that Caesar had killed the Aeduan leaders, and led them into revolt (Caesar, BG VII.37-40). Discovered, he fled to Gergovia and was one of those who drew the Aedui to the side of Vercingetorix.

personas/convictolitavis/resumen.texto: Aeduan noble whom Caesar, as arbiter, confirmed as vergobret (the annual supreme magistrate) of the Aedui in 52 BC against his rival Cotus (BG VII.32-33). Shortly afterward, bribed by the Arverni according to Caesar, he joined the revolt.

personas/eporedorix/resumen.texto: Young Aeduan noble who in 52 BC denounced Litaviccus's treachery to Caesar and then, together with Viridomarus, led the Aedui into revolt (BG VII.39, VII.54-55); he was one of the four leaders of the relief army at Alesia (VII.76), and what became of him is not known. Caesar also mentions an older Aeduan Eporedorix, captured in the cavalry battle before Alesia (VII.67).

personas/vercasivelauno/resumen.texto: Arvernian, cousin of Vercingetorix, one of the four leaders of the relief army at Alesia. He led the main attack against the Roman camp on the north and was captured (Caesar, BG VII.76, VII.83-88).

personas/critognato/resumen.texto: Arvernian noble besieged at Alesia, to whom Caesar (BG VII.77) attributes a speech proposing that those unable to fight be eaten rather than surrender, as the ancestors had done against the Cimbri. Caesar says he records it for its “singular and ill-omened cruelty”; many historians read it as a speech composed by Caesar, in the manner of ancient historians, that both condemns the Gauls and explains their resistance.

personas/camulogeno/resumen.texto: Elderly chief of the Aulerci, to whom the Parisii and their neighbors gave command in 52 BC for his military experience; he died fighting Labienus near Lutetia (Caesar, BG VII.57-62).

personas/teutomato/resumen.texto: King of the Nitiobroges, son of Olovicon, whom the Senate had called “friend”, who joined Vercingetorix in 52 BC. Caesar (BG VII.31, VII.46) tells that in the attack on Gergovia he was caught napping during the afternoon rest and escaped half-naked on a wounded horse.

personas/gutuatro/resumen.texto: Chief of the Carnutes who in 52 BC, according to Caesar (BG VII.3, where he appears as Cotuatus, together with Conconnetodumnus), gave the signal for the massacre of Roman traders at Cenabum. In 51 BC he was handed over, and Caesar had him flogged to death and beheaded because his soldiers demanded it (Hirtius, BG VIII.38). Some authors read his name as “gutuater”, a priestly title known from inscriptions, and count him among Gaulish priests; this is a hypothesis.

personas/lucterio/resumen.texto: Cadurcian, lieutenant of Vercingetorix, who in 52 BC carried the revolt to southern Gaul and in 51 BC shut himself up with Drappes in Uxellodunum (Caesar, BG VII.5-8; Hirtius, BG VIII.30-44). He escaped the siege, but the Arvernian Epasnactus, an ally of Rome, handed him over to Caesar.

personas/drapes/resumen.texto: Senone who in 51 BC gathered fugitives and freed slaves and joined Lucterius to attack the Province; captured near Uxellodunum, he let himself starve to death (Hirtius, BG VIII.30-44).

personas/correo/resumen.texto: Chief of the Bellovaci who in 51 BC, together with the Atrebatan Commius, led the last great resistance in northern Gaul. According to Hirtius (BG VIII.6-19) he fell fighting after refusing to surrender.

personas/dumnaco/resumen.texto: Chief of the Andes who in 51 BC besieged Lemonum (Poitiers), defended by an ally of Rome, and was defeated by the legates Caninius and Fabius; he fled to the edge of Gaul and nothing more was heard of him (Hirtius, BG VIII.26-31).

personas/epasnacto/resumen.texto: Arvernian ally of Rome who in 51 BC captured the Cadurcian Lucterius and handed him over to Caesar (Hirtius, BG VIII.44). It shows that the Arvernian aristocracy remained divided even after Alesia.

personas/tito-labieno/resumen.texto: Caesar's chief legate in Gaul, who commanded the army in his absence, defeated Indutiomarus, the Treveri and Camulogenus near Lutetia (Caesar, BG V-VII). In 49 BC he went over to Pompey's side and died at the battle of Munda.

personas/quinto-tulio-ciceron/resumen.texto: Brother of the orator Cicero and legate of Caesar, who in 54 BC held out in his winter camp against the siege by the Nervii and the Eburones until Caesar came to his aid (BG V.38-52). He died in the proscriptions of 43 BC.

personas/quinto-titurio-sabino/resumen.texto: Caesar's legate who in 56 BC defeated Viridovix and in 54 BC accepted Ambiorix's offer to leave the camp at Atuatuca; he died in the ambush with most of his troops (BG V.26-37). Caesar lays the full blame for the disaster on him.

personas/lucio-aurunculeio-cota/resumen.texto: Caesar's legate who shared command of the camp at Atuatuca and, according to Caesar (BG V.28-37), opposed leaving it; he died fighting in Ambiorix's ambush.

personas/publio-licinio-craso/resumen.texto: Son of the triumvir Crassus and an officer of Caesar who in 57 BC subdued the peoples of Armorica and in 56 BC conquered Aquitania (BG III.20-27). He died in 53 BC with his father in the defeat at Carrhae against the Parthians.

personas/decimo-junio-bruto-albino/resum.texto: Officer of Caesar who in 56 BC commanded the fleet that destroyed the Veneti in the Gulf of Morbihan (BG III.14-15). He was one of Caesar's assassins in 44 BC and died the following year.

personas/claudio/resumen.texto: Roman emperor (41-54) born in Lugdunum, who conquered Britain and in 48 argued before the Senate that the nobles of Gallia Comata should be eligible to become senators; the speech survives on the Lyon Claudian tablet and in Tacitus's version (Annals XI.23-25). According to Suetonius (Claudius 25) he banned the religion of the druids, although Pliny (XXX.13) attributes the measure to Tiberius. Ancient sources, especially Suetonius and Seneca, ridicule him; modern historians value his government more highly.

personas/julio-floro/resumen.texto: Treveran noble, a Roman citizen, who in 21 led with the Aeduan Julius Sacrovir a revolt of Gallic cities burdened by debt (Tacitus, Annals III.40-42). He was defeated by Roman troops and by another Treveran, Julius Indus, and killed himself.

personas/julio-indo/resumen.texto: Treveran noble, rival of Julius Florus, who in 21 helped the Romans disperse the rebels at the head of a picked force (Tacitus, Annals III.42). Inscriptions later record an “ala Indiana”, a Gallic cavalry unit bearing his name. It shows that the Gallic aristocracies were divided over Rome.

personas/julio-sacroviro/resumen.texto: Aeduan noble, a Roman citizen, who in 21 rebelled with the Treveran Julius Florus against debts and taxes; he took Augustodunum with the sons of the Gallic nobility who studied there and armed armored gladiators, the “crupellarii”. Defeated by Gaius Silius, he killed himself in a country house that he had set on fire (Tacitus, Annals III.40-46).

personas/julio-vindex/resumen.texto: Governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, descendant of Aquitanian kings and a senator, who in March 68 rebelled against Nero and offered the empire to Galba. The Rhine legions defeated him near Vesontio and he killed himself (Cassius Dio LXIII.22-25; Plutarch, Galba 4-6). Nineteenth-century historians saw his revolt as a national Gallic uprising; since Peter Brunt's study (1959) it has been considered mainly a rebellion of the Roman aristocracy against Nero.

personas/marico/resumen.texto: Boian of humble origin who in 69 proclaimed himself “liberator of the Gauls” and a god, gathered eight thousand peasants and was crushed by the militia of the Aedui. Tacitus (Histories II.61) tells that they threw him to the beasts, which did not touch him, and that he was executed in the presence of Vitellius. He is one of the few Gallic popular movements of which we have any record.

personas/julio-civil/resumen.texto: Batavian prince, a Roman citizen and commander of auxiliary troops, who in 69 led the Batavian revolt against Rome, at first under the pretext of supporting Vespasian. He allied with the Treveri and the Lingones of the “Empire of the Gauls” and was defeated by Petilius Cerialis in 70. Tacitus (Histories IV-V), the only source, breaks off the account during his peace negotiations, and it is not known how he ended.

personas/julio-clasico/resumen.texto: Treveran who claimed descent from kings, prefect of a cavalry wing, who in 70 proclaimed with Julius Tutor and Julius Sabinus the “Empire of the Gauls” and won the oath of loyalty of two Roman legions (Tacitus, Histories IV.55-59). Defeated by Petilius Cerialis, he fled with Civilis across the Rhine.

personas/julio-tutor/resumen.texto: Treveran, prefect of the Rhine bank by appointment of Vitellius, who in 70 joined Classicus in the “Empire of the Gauls” and was defeated by the Romans at Bingium and Trier (Tacitus, Histories IV.55-78).

personas/julio-sabino/resumen.texto: Lingonian noble who claimed descent from a great-grandmother who had been a lover of Julius Caesar, and in 70 proclaimed himself Caesar of the “Empire of the Gauls” (Tacitus, Histories IV.55, IV.67). Defeated by the Sequani, he faked his death and lived for nine years hidden in a tomb with his wife Epponina; when discovered, he was executed in Rome on Vespasian's orders (Plutarch, Erotikos 25; Cassius Dio LXVI.16).

personas/eponina/resumen.texto: Wife of Julius Sabinus, who hid him for nine years in an underground refuge, had two children there, and traveled to Rome with him to plead for pardon. According to Plutarch (Erotikos 25), who met one of their sons, she told Vespasian that she had been happier underground than he was on the throne; she was executed in 79 (Cassius Dio LXVI.16; Tacitus, Histories IV.67). She is the Gallic woman with the greatest presence in the sources, which present her as a model of marital fidelity, a Roman and Greek ideal.

personas/vespasiano/resumen.texto: Roman emperor (69-79) who won the civil war of 69 and whose reign ended the Batavian revolt and the “Empire of the Gauls” in 70. He ordered the execution of Julius Sabinus and Epponina in 79 (Cassius Dio LXVI.16). Earlier he had served in the conquest of Britain and commanded the war in Judea.

personas/postumo/resumen.texto: General of Gallic or Batavian origin who in 260 proclaimed himself emperor in Gaul and founded the so-called Gallic Empire, which governed Gaul, Britain and for a time Hispania from Colonia and Trier. He defended the Rhine against the Franks and Alamanni and was killed by his own soldiers in 269. The sources are brief (Aurelius Victor, Eutropius, the Historia Augusta), and historians debate whether his empire was separatist or a way of protecting the Roman order.

personas/ireneo-de-lyon/resumen.texto: Bishop of Lugdunum of Greek origin, a disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna, who wrote Against Heresies around 180. In the preface he apologizes for his style, saying that he lives among the Celts and often uses “a barbarian tongue”, one of the testimonies that Gaulish was still spoken in Lyon at the end of the 2nd century.

personas/greg-woolf/resumen.texto: British historian of Rome, author of Becoming Roman (1998), who studied Roman Gaul as a process of cultural change driven by local elites rather than as the imposition of a fixed Roman culture.

personas/david-henige/resumen.texto: American historian and librarian at the University of Wisconsin, a specialist in the critique of demographic figures from antiquity and the colonial period. In “He came, he saw, we counted” (1998) he analyzed Caesar's figures for Gaul.

personas/leon-fleuriot/resumen.texto: Breton Celticist, author of a dictionary of Old Breton and of Les origines de la Bretagne (1980), where he argued that Breton arose from the contact between the Brittonic of the 4th-to-6th-century immigrants and a Gaulish that was still alive in Armorica.

personas/kurt-raaflaub/resumen.texto: Swiss historian of antiquity, professor at Brown University and editor of Caesar's Commentaries in the Landmark series. In “Caesar and Genocide” (2021) he discussed whether Caesar's campaigns in Gaul can be called genocidal.

personas/iccio/resumen.texto: Remi noble who in 57 BC, together with Andecombogius, went to offer Caesar his people's submission and informed him about the forces of the Belgic coalition (BG II.3-6); afterward he defended the oppidum of Bibrax against the Belgae. From then on the Remi were Rome's main allies in the north.

personas/vertico/resumen.texto: Nervian refugee in the camp of Quintus Cicero during the siege of 54 BC, whose Gallic slave carried to Caesar, hidden in a javelin, the letter asking for help (BG V.45). Caesar presents him as a loyal ally.

personas/gobanicio/resumen.texto: Uncle of Vercingetorix who, with other Arvernian nobles opposed to the war, expelled him from Gergovia at the beginning of 52 BC; shortly afterward Vercingetorix returned with his supporters and in turn drove him out (Caesar, BG VII.4).

personas/coto/resumen.texto: Aeduan noble who in 52 BC contested the office of vergobret with Convictolitavis; Caesar ruled against him because his election had not been held according to Aeduan law (BG VII.32-33). He was captured as commander of the Aeduan cavalry in the battle before Alesia (VII.67).

personas/viridomaro-eduo/resumen.texto: Young Aeduan of humble origin whom Caesar himself says he had promoted (BG VII.39), and who in 52 BC led the Aedui into revolt together with Eporedorix, sacked Noviodunum (Nevers) with the hostages and treasure of Caesar (VII.54-55), and was one of the four leaders of the relief army at Alesia (VII.76). What became of him is not known.

personas/cayo-valerio-procilo/resumen.texto: Noble of the Helvii of the Province, son of Caburus, who had received Roman citizenship from the governor Gaius Valerius Flaccus; Caesar calls him “a young man of great courage and culture” (BG I.47). In 58 BC he acted as interpreter between Caesar and the druid Diviciacus (I.19, where the manuscripts give the form Troucillus) and was sent to Ariovistus, who had him put in chains on suspicion of being a spy; after the battle he was found alive, and he told how the Germans had cast lots three times to decide whether to burn him (I.53). He is one of the few Gauls whose Roman citizenship and people of origin are both known.

personas/lucio-munacio-planco/resumen.texto: Legate of Caesar in Gaul and later governor of Gallia Comata, who in 43 BC founded the colony of Lugdunum (Cassius Dio XLVI.50) and, according to his epitaph from Gaeta, also that of Raurica (Augst). He changed sides several times during the civil wars and in 27 BC proposed in the Senate the title Augustus for Octavian (Suetonius, Augustus 7).

personas/cayo-julio-vercondaridubno/resu.texto: Aeduan noble named first priest of the altar of Rome and Augustus at the confluence of the Rhône and the Saône, dedicated in 12 BC, according to Livy's Periocha 139, which in the same passage mentions a disturbance in Gaul over the census. His name joins the family name of Caesar with a Gaulish name and shows how Rome integrated the Gallic nobility into the imperial cult.

personas/cayo-julio-rufo/resumen.texto: Roman citizen of the Santones and priest of Rome and Augustus at the altar of Lugdunum, who in 18 or 19 paid for the arch of Germanicus at Saintes. The inscription on the arch names his father, Gaius Julius Otuaneunus, his grandfather, Gaius Julius Gedomo, and his great-grandfather Epotsoviridus, who has only a Gaulish name: four generations that show a noble Gallic family passing to Roman citizenship while keeping its Gaulish names. An inscription also credits him with works in the amphitheatre of the Three Gauls at Lyon.

personas/decimo-valerio-asiatico/resumen.texto: Senator born in Vienne, in Narbonensis, consul in 35 and 46: the first Gaul to reach the consulship. In 47 Claudius forced him to kill himself at the instigation of Messalina (Tacitus, Annals XI.1-3). In the speech on the Claudian tablet, a year later, Claudius contemptuously alludes to an unnamed senator from Vienne, and most editors understand this to be him.

hechos/llegada-de-los-galos-a-italia/tit.texto: The Gauls settle in the Po valley

hechos/llegada-de-los-galos-a-italia/res.texto: Livy (V.33-35) gives two versions: the migration of Belovesus in the time of Tarquinius Priscus, around 600 BC, and the invitation of Aruns of Clusium, who is said to have lured the Gauls with wine to take revenge on the seducer of his wife; Polybius (II.17) says only that the Celts coveted the plain of the Etruscans and drove them out, and lists the Insubres, Cenomani, Boii, Lingones and Senones. Archaeology shows that a Celtic language, Lepontic, was spoken in the lake region from the 6th century BC (Golasecca culture), and that La Tène objects and Gallic cemeteries spread through the Po valley and the Adriatic coast from the early 4th century BC. Some historians propose that Livy's early date and Polybius's date reflect those two stages; others see in Belovesus a legend of origin with no chronological value. The Aruns anecdote is considered an Etruscan-Roman legend.

hechos/caida-de-melpum/titulo.texto: The Insubres, Boii and Senones take Melpum

hechos/caida-de-melpum/resumen.texto: Pliny (III.125), citing Cornelius Nepos, says that the wealthy Etruscan city of Melpum, in the Po plain, was destroyed by the Insubres, Boii and Senones on the same day that Camillus took Veii (396 BC). It is the only dated record of the Gallic conquest of Cisalpine Etruria; Melpum has not been identified with certainty, and the synchronism may be a construction of the chroniclers.

hechos/saqueo-galo-de-roma/titulo.texto: The Gauls win at the Allia and sack Rome

hechos/saqueo-galo-de-roma/resumen.texto: According to Livy (V.35-49), the Senones of Brennus besieged Clusium; the Roman envoys, three Fabii, fought against them in violation of the law of nations, and the Gauls marched on Rome, defeated the Romans by the river Allia on 18 July, a day that became a day of ill omen, and sacked the city, except for the Capitol, defended by Manlius and the geese of Juno; Rome paid a thousand pounds of gold, Brennus said “vae victis”, and Camillus arrived in time to defeat them. Polybius (II.18, II.22), who is older, does not mention Camillus: he says that the Gauls made a pact, returned the city and went back unbeaten with their booty because the Veneti were invading their lands, which makes Camillus's victory a Roman patriotic account; Diodorus (XIV.117) says that Camillus defeated them later, when they were besieging Veascium, and recovered the gold, and Strabo (V.2.3) attributes that victory to the people of Caere. The traditional date, 390 BC, is that of Varro's chronology; Polybius's synchronism with the peace of Antalcidas gives 387-386 BC, which many historians now prefer. Archaeology has found no level of general destruction attributable to the sack (the burnt layer of the Comitium once assigned to it dates from the 6th century BC), so the real damage is disputed; the trauma, however, marked the Roman image of the Gaul for centuries.

hechos/duelo-de-manlio-torcuato/titulo.texto: The duel of Manlius Torquatus with a Gaul

hechos/duelo-de-manlio-torcuato/resumen.texto: According to Livy (VII.9-10) and the annalist Claudius Quadrigarius, cited by Aulus Gellius (IX.13), a giant Gaul challenged the Romans by the bridge over the Anio, and the young Titus Manlius killed him and took his torque, from which came the cognomen Torquatus. It is an exemplary story of the annalists, built on the contrast between the huge, disorderly Gaul and the disciplined Roman; it also shows that the Gauls were still raiding Latium in the mid-4th century BC.

hechos/duelo-de-valerio-corvo/titulo.texto: The duel of Valerius Corvus with a Gaul

hechos/duelo-de-valerio-corvo/resumen.texto: According to Livy (VII.26), a military tribune, Marcus Valerius, defeated a Gallic chief in single combat with the help of a crow that landed on his helmet and attacked the enemy's face. The story, which explains the cognomen Corvus, is legendary; Polybius (II.18) says only that in those years the Gauls attacked again and that Rome ended up signing a thirty-year peace with them, around 334 BC.

hechos/batalla-de-sentino/resumen.texto: Rome defeated at Sentinum, in Umbria, a coalition of Samnites and Gallic Senones (the Etruscans and Umbrians did not fight), in the largest battle of Italy in its time. Livy (X.27-30) tells of the “devotio” of the consul Publius Decius Mus, who threw himself to his death to win victory for his men, and gives 25,000 enemy dead and 8,000 prisoners (X.29), while criticizing the authors who inflated the size of the enemy army (X.30); Duris of Samos, cited by Diodorus (XXI.6), spoke of a hundred thousand dead. The victory opened the way to Roman domination of central Italy.

hechos/batalla-de-arretium/resumen.texto: According to Polybius (II.19), the Senones besieged Arretium and destroyed the army of the praetor Lucius Caecilius Metellus, who died in the battle; afterward they killed the envoys Rome sent to negotiate about the prisoners. The killing of the envoys provoked Roman reprisals against the Senones.

hechos/expulsion-de-los-senones/titulo.texto: Rome expels the Senones and founds Sena Gallica

hechos/expulsion-de-los-senones/resumen.texto: In reprisal for Arretium, Manius Curius Dentatus laid waste the territory of the Senones on the Adriatic coast, and Rome expelled them and founded the colony of Sena Gallica there (Polybius II.19). Polybius says that it was the first Gallic territory in Italy from which Rome drove out the inhabitants; the “ager Gallicus” became public Roman land.

hechos/batalla-del-lago-vadimon/resumen.texto: The Boii and the Etruscans, who had marched together against Rome after the expulsion of the Senones, were defeated by the consul Publius Cornelius Dolabella near Lake Vadimo, in Etruria (Polybius II.20). The following year the Boii were defeated again and asked for peace, which lasted about forty-five years.

hechos/ley-agraria-de-flaminio/titulo.texto: Flaminius's law distributes the ager Gallicus

hechos/ley-agraria-de-flaminio/resumen.texto: The tribune Gaius Flaminius had the former territory of the Senones divided into plots for Roman citizens. Polybius (II.21), who writes from the viewpoint of the Roman aristocracy, presents it as the beginning of the corruption of the people and the reason why the Boii and the Insubres, fearing the same fate, prepared the great invasion of 225 BC.

hechos/batalla-de-telamon/resumen.texto: The Insubres and Boii, with the Gesatae from beyond the Alps, invaded Etruria with 50,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry according to Polybius (II.23), defeated the Romans near Faesulae and were trapped at Telamon between two consular armies. Polybius (II.28-31) describes the Gesatae fighting naked, wearing gold necklaces and armbands, with the noise of their trumpets and horns, and gives 40,000 Gauls dead and 10,000 prisoners, among them King Concolitanus; King Aneroestus killed himself, and the consul Gaius Atilius Regulus also died. The scene is the basis of the Greco-Roman image of the Gallic warrior; the figures are those of a Roman source that Polybius follows.

hechos/batalla-de-clastidio/resumen.texto: The consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus defeated the Insubres and Gesatae who were besieging Clastidium and killed their leader Viridomarus in single combat, and he dedicated the arms as “spolia opima” (Plutarch, Marcellus 6-8; Polybius II.34). That same year the Romans took Mediolanum, the main city of the Insubres, which surrendered.

hechos/galos-en-el-ejercito-de-anibal/ti.texto: The Gauls of Cisalpine Gaul join Hannibal

hechos/galos-en-el-ejercito-de-anibal/re.texto: When Rome founded the colonies of Placentia and Cremona in 218 BC, the Boii and the Insubres rebelled and attacked the colonists; shortly afterward Hannibal crossed the Alps and the Gauls joined him (Polybius III.40, III.66-69; Livy XXI.25). They formed a large part of his army at the Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae, where they formed the center with the Iberians, and Polybius (III.117) reports about four thousand Gauls dead. Roman sources present them as inconstant allies, an image that also served to explain Hannibal's failures.

hechos/arbitraje-de-las-mujeres-celtas/t.texto: Celtic women as arbiters in the treaty with Hannibal

hechos/arbitraje-de-las-mujeres-celtas/r.texto: Plutarch (Virtues of Women 6) tells that, before Hannibal crossed Gaul, the women of the Celts had halted a civil war among them, and that since then they deliberated on war and peace and arbitrated with the allies; the treaty with Hannibal established that a Celt's complaints against a Carthaginian were judged by the Carthaginian leaders, and a Carthaginian's complaints against a Celt by Celtic women. Livy (XXI.24) places Hannibal's meeting with the Gallic chiefs at Ruscino, without mentioning women. It is an isolated testimony, which some historians take as evidence of a public role for women and others as a moralizing anecdote by Plutarch; it does not support speaking of “matriarchy”.

hechos/batalla-de-la-selva-litana/resume.texto: The Boii ambushed the consul-elect Lucius Postumius Albinus in a forest of the Po valley and destroyed his army. Livy (XXIII.24) says that they cut off Postumius's head, cleaned it, covered it with gold and used it as a sacred cup in a temple; it is one of the central texts on the Gallic cult of heads, for which archaeology provides indications in other places, such as Entremont and Roquepertuse.

hechos/batalla-de-cremona-200/resumen.texto: A coalition of Insubres, Boii and Cenomani, led according to Livy (XXXI.10, XXXI.21) by the Carthaginian Hamilcar, who had stayed in Italy after Hannibal, sacked Placentia and was defeated by the praetor Lucius Furius Purpurio before Cremona. Livy gives 35,000 Gauls killed or captured, a figure that cannot be verified.

hechos/conquista-de-la-galia-cisalpina/r.texto: After the Second Punic War, Rome subdued the Insubres and Cenomani (197-194 BC), and in 191 BC Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica defeated the Boii, whose land Livy (XXXVI.38-40) says he took half of; Polybius (II.35) and Strabo (V.1.6) say they were expelled, and it is debated whether the Boii of Bohemia and the Danube are in part their descendants. Colonies were founded in the plain (Bononia in 189, Parma and Mutina in 183) and the Via Aemilia was laid out; the inhabitants received Latin rights in 89 BC, Roman citizenship with Caesar in 49 BC, and the region was joined to Italy in 42 BC. Polybius (II.35) says he recounted these wars so that the Greeks would not be frightened by barbarian invasions; J. H. C. Williams argues that much of the account of a permanent “Gallic danger” is a Roman literary construction.

hechos/deportacion-de-los-ligures-apuano.texto: Rome deports the Apuan Ligurians to Samnium

After more than half a century of wars against the Ligurians of the Apennines, the consuls Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Bebius Tanfilus deported 40,000 Apuan Ligurians with their wives and children to public land in Samnium, and the following year another 7,000 (Livy XL.38, XL.41). There they formed the communities of the Ligures Baebiani and Corneliani, also known from inscriptions. It is one of the earliest documented mass deportations of Roman expansion.

hechos/destruccion-de-entremont/titulo.texto: Rome destroys Entremont and founds Aquae Sextiae

hechos/destruccion-de-entremont/resumen.texto: Massalia asked Rome for help against the Salluvii in 125 BC; the consul Marcus Fulvius Flaccus and then Gaius Sextius Calvinus defeated them, destroyed their oppidum of Entremont and in 122 BC founded a garrison at its foot, Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence), according to the epitomes of Livy (Periochae 60-61) and Strabo (IV.1.5). The king of the Salluvii, Teutomalius, fled to the Allobroges, which gave the reason for the next war. The archaeology of Entremont shows a violent destruction and a last brief period of occupation.

hechos/batalla-de-vindalio/resumen.texto: The proconsul Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus defeated the Allobroges at Vindalium, near the confluence of the Sorgue and the Rhône, partly thanks to war elephants, which frightened the Gauls (Orosius V.13; Livy, Periocha 61). It was the first step of the war that led to the creation of the province.

hechos/derrota-de-bituito/titulo.texto: Battle of the Isère: defeat of Bituitus

hechos/derrota-de-bituito/lugar.texto: Confluence of the Isère and the Rhône

hechos/derrota-de-bituito/resumen.texto: The consul Quintus Fabius Maximus defeated the Arverni of King Bituitus and the Allobroges at the confluence of the Isère and the Rhône; the epitomes of Livy (Periocha 61) and Orosius (V.14) give more than a hundred thousand Gauls dead, figures that cannot be verified. Bituitus was captured shortly afterward by treachery and sent to Rome; this ended the Arvernian hegemony over Gaul that Strabo describes (IV.2.3).

hechos/fundacion-de-la-narbonense/titulo.texto: Rome creates the province of southern Gaul

hechos/fundacion-de-la-narbonense/resume.texto: After the victories over the Allobroges and the Arverni, Rome organized a province between the Alps and the Pyrenees, linked by the Via Domitia, and founded the colony of Narbo Martius around 118 BC. It was first called “the Province” (hence Provence) and, from Augustus, Narbonensis. Cicero, defending the governor Fonteius (around 69 BC), reveals the abuses of tax collectors and traders and disparages the testimony of the Gauls for being barbarians.

hechos/alobroges-delatan-a-catilina/resu.texto: An embassy of the Allobroges, which had gone to Rome to complain about debts and the abuses of governors, received from Catiline's conspirators a proposal to raise their people in revolt; the envoys told their Roman patron and gave Cicero the letters that proved the conspiracy (Sallust, Catiline 40-45; Plutarch, Cicero 18). Two years later the Allobroges, having received nothing, rebelled under Catugnatus.

hechos/revuelta-de-catugnato/resumen.texto: The Allobroges, in debt and pressed by the tax collectors, rose up under Catugnatus and were defeated by the governor Gaius Pomptinus (Cassius Dio XXXVII.47-48). It was the last revolt in the Province before Caesar's arrival.

hechos/sitio-de-masalia/resumen.texto: Massalia, an ally of Rome for four centuries, closed its gates to Caesar during the civil war and supported Pompey; Gaius Trebonius and Decimus Brutus besieged it by land and sea, and it surrendered after several months (Caesar, Civil War I.34-36, II.1-22; Cassius Dio XLI.19-25). It kept its nominal autonomy but lost almost all its territory to new colonies such as Arelate. Lucan (Pharsalia III) describes the felling of a sacred grove during the siege.

hechos/guerra-cimbria/resumen.texto: The Cimbri and the Teutones, peoples who had come from northern Europe, wandered for more than ten years through Noricum, Gaul and Hispania with their families, defeated several Roman armies, and were destroyed by Marius at Aquae Sextiae (102 BC) and Vercellae (101 BC), according to Plutarch (Marius 11-27) and the epitomes of Livy. Strabo (VII.2.1-3) places them on the Jutland peninsula, and Augustus (Res gestae 26) received a Cimbrian embassy there. Caesar presents them as a precedent for Ariovistus' Germans (BG I.33, I.40), but Posidonius and Diodorus counted them among the Celts, and the names of their leaders (Boiorix, Gesorix, Lugio) are Celtic: today they are generally considered Germanic peoples of Jutland with strong Celtic contacts, although the debate remains open. In Rome they left behind the fear of the “Cimbrian terror.”

hechos/batalla-de-noreia/resumen.texto: The consul Gnaeus Papirius Carbo treacherously attacked the Cimbri as they entered Noricum and was defeated near Noreia; only a storm saved his army from total destruction (Appian, Celtica 13; Strabo V.1.8). It was Rome's first clash with the Cimbri.

hechos/batalla-de-burdigala/titulo.texto: The Tigurini defeat Lucius Cassius Longinus

hechos/batalla-de-burdigala/resumen.texto: The Tigurini, a pagus of the Helvetii allied with the Cimbri, defeated and killed the consul Lucius Cassius Longinus in the territory of the Nitiobroges and forced the survivors to pass under the yoke (Livy, Periocha 65; Caesar, BG I.7, I.12). Caesar, who was related by marriage to one of the victims, uses the defeat to justify his attack on the Helvetii in 58 BC.

hechos/batalla-de-arausio/resumen.texto: The Cimbri and Teutones destroyed near Arausio the armies of Caepio and Gnaeus Mallius Maximus, who refused to fight together. Livy's Periocha 67 gives 80,000 soldiers and 40,000 servants dead, but notes that it follows the annalist Valerius Antias, whom Livy himself reproaches in other books for inflating figures; it was the greatest Roman defeat since Cannae according to the ancients, but the number cannot be verified. Caepio was condemned and his property confiscated. The disaster led to Marius being elected consul five years running.

hechos/batalla-de-aquae-sextiae/resumen.texto: Marius waited for the Teutones and Ambrones in a fortified camp and defeated them in two days of fighting near Aquae Sextiae; Plutarch (Marius 21) gives more than a hundred thousand dead or captured, and Livy's Periocha 68 gives two hundred thousand dead and ninety thousand prisoners; these figures cannot be verified. Plutarch (Marius 19) tells that the Ligurians in the Roman army, hearing the Ambrones shout their name, shouted the same thing, because they too were called that, and that the Ambrone women attacked with axes those who were fleeing. King Teutobodus was captured.

hechos/batalla-de-vercelas/resumen.texto: Marius and Quintus Lutatius Catulus defeated the Cimbri in the Raudine Fields, near Vercellae, and King Boiorix was killed (Orosius V.16); Plutarch (Marius 27) gives more than 60,000 prisoners and twice as many dead, and Livy's Periocha 68 gives 140,000 dead and 60,000 prisoners. Plutarch tells that the Cimbrian women, dressed in black, killed from their wagons those who fled, strangled their children, and hanged themselves before falling into captivity; it is a literary scene that serves the image of the ferocious barbarian, but also one of the few testimonies about the women of these peoples, who accompanied the army with their families.

hechos/batalla-de-magetobriga/titulo.texto: Ariovistus defeats the Aedui at Magetobriga

hechos/batalla-de-magetobriga/resumen.texto: The Sequani and the Arverni, rivals of the Aedui, called in the Suebian king Ariovistus as a mercenary; he crossed the Rhine with thousands of Germans and defeated the Aedui at Magetobriga. Afterward he took a third of the lands of the Sequani and demanded another third (Caesar, BG I.31, Diviciacus' speech). We know the battle only through Caesar, who uses it to present Ariovistus as a threat to all of Gaul.

hechos/conjura-de-orgetorix/resumen.texto: According to Caesar (BG I.2-4), the Helvetian noble Orgetorix persuaded his people to emigrate toward western Gaul and made a pact with the Sequanian Casticus and the Aeduan Dumnorix to make themselves kings of their three peoples and dominate Gaul. The Helvetii put him on trial for aspiring to kingship, a crime they punished by burning at the stake, and he died before the verdict. The story shows, according to Caesar, that in these communities power lay in the hands of assemblies and magistrates and that kingship was viewed with suspicion.

hechos/guerra-de-las-galias-hecho/resume.texto: In eight campaigns, between 58 and 50 BC, Julius Caesar conquered all of Gaul between the Pyrenees, the Rhine and the ocean, in a war that began against the Helvetii and Ariovistus, continued with the Belgae, the Veneti and the Aquitanians, crossed the Rhine and the Channel toward Britain, and culminated in the revolt of Vercingetorix and the siege of Alesia (52 BC). Almost everything we know comes from Caesar's own Commentaries, written to defend his career before Rome and completed by Hirtius. Plutarch (Caesar 15) says he fought against three million men, killed one million and enslaved another million; Velleius Paterculus (II.47) gives more than 400,000 dead and more prisoners, and Pliny (VII.92) gives 1,192,000 dead in all of Caesar's battles, not only in Gaul, excluding the civil wars. These figures ultimately come from Caesar, and David Henige (1998) argues that they cannot be verified; the population of Gaul is also unknown, and according to modern estimates that Raaflaub (2021) considers reasonable it could have reached 8, 10 or 12 million. That the mortality and enslavement were massive is not disputed; Kurt Raaflaub and Nico Roymans argue that episodes such as the massacre of the Usipetes and Tencteri or the devastation of the country of the Eburones fit the modern definition of genocide, while others point out that the category is anachronistic and that there is no way to measure the fall in population.

hechos/migracion-de-los-helvecios/resume.texto: In March 58 BC the Helvetii burned their twelve oppida and four hundred villages and set out, with the Tulingi, Latobrigi, Rauraci and Boii, on a migration toward the land of the Santones. Caesar blocked their way through the Province, pursued them and defeated them at Bibracte, and forced them to return (BG I.2-29). Caesar (BG I.29) says that in his camp they found tablets in Greek letters with the census of the emigrants: 368,000 people, 92,000 of them in arms, of whom 110,000 returned. Henige (1998) and others point out that these figures cannot be verified, that they depend on a document no one else saw, and that the motive Caesar attributes to the migration (the ambition of Orgetorix) served to justify the war; pressure from the northern Germans is the other cause historians give.

hechos/batalla-del-arar/resumen.texto: Caesar attacked by surprise the Tigurini, a quarter of the Helvetii, while they were crossing the Arar (Saône), and destroyed them (BG I.12). He says that this avenged both a public and a private offense: the defeat of Cassius Longinus in 107 BC and the death of his father-in-law's grandfather.

hechos/batalla-de-bibracte/resumen.texto: Near the Aeduan oppidum of Bibracte, Caesar defeated the Helvetii and their allies, who fought until nightfall and held out among their wagons, where women and children also fought (BG I.23-26). Some 130,000 survivors fled toward the Lingones; Caesar forced them to return to their land so that the Germans would not occupy it, and let the Boii settle among the Aedui.

hechos/batalla-de-los-vosgos/resumen.texto: After a failed interview, in which Ariovistus said that Gaul was as much his as the Province was Rome's, Caesar defeated him on the plain of Alsace; the Germans fled to the Rhine, and the king's two wives and one of his daughters died (BG I.30-54). Caesar (BG I.50) tells that German matrons had announced by divination that they should not fight before the new moon. The exact location of the battle is disputed.

hechos/batalla-del-axona/resumen.texto: The Belgae, allied against Caesar under King Galba of the Suessiones, attacked the Roman camp by the Axona (Aisne) after the Remi had gone over to Rome; they failed, ran out of supplies and dispersed (BG II.1-11). Caesar then subdued the Suessiones, Bellovaci and Ambiani one by one.

hechos/batalla-del-sabis/resumen.texto: The Nervii of Boduognatus, with the Atrebates and Viromandui, attacked the legions by surprise while they were setting up camp by the Sabis, and Caesar had to fight in the front line to avoid defeat (BG II.16-28). He says that of 60,000 Nervii only 500 remained, and of 600 senators three; three years later the Nervii again besieged a Roman camp with a large army, a contradiction that critics use to show how much his figures are exaggerated.

hechos/sitio-de-los-atuatucos/titulo.texto: Siege and sale of the Atuatuci

hechos/sitio-de-los-atuatucos/resumen.texto: The Atuatuci, who according to Caesar descended from the Cimbri and Teutones, surrendered, attempted a night attack while hiding part of their weapons, and were defeated. Caesar sold all the inhabitants of the oppidum, 53,000 people according to the buyers (BG II.29-33). It is the first mass sale of prisoners recorded in the war, and shows the importance of the slave trade in the conquest.

hechos/campana-contra-los-venetos/resume.texto: The Veneti, the seafaring people of Armorica who controlled trade with Britain, held Roman officers sent to demand grain. Caesar built a fleet on the Loire, and Decimus Brutus defeated them in the Gulf of Morbihan by cutting the halyards of their leather sails with sickles (BG III.7-16). Caesar had their senate executed and sold the rest of the population “so that the barbarians would respect the law of ambassadors.” That year Sabinus also defeated Viridovix and the Unelli.

hechos/campana-de-aquitania/resumen.texto: The young Publius Crassus subdued the Sotiates of King Adiatuanus and a coalition of Aquitanian peoples aided by Cantabrians who had fought with Sertorius (BG III.20-27). Caesar says that of 50,000 enemies barely a quarter escaped. The Aquitanians, according to Caesar (BG I.1), differed from the Gauls in language and customs; later inscriptions confirm that they spoke a language related to Basque.

hechos/masacre-de-usipetes-y-tencteros/t.texto: Massacre of the Usipetes and Tencteri

hechos/masacre-de-usipetes-y-tencteros/l.texto: Kessel-Lith (confluence of the Meuse and the Waal)

hechos/masacre-de-usipetes-y-tencteros/r.texto: The Usipetes and Tencteri, Germanic peoples expelled by the Suebi, crossed the lower Rhine with their families. Caesar held back their leaders, who had come to negotiate, and attacked the camp, where men, women and children died. Caesar (BG IV.14-15) says there were 430,000 people, that the cavalry pursued women and children and that many drowned in the river, with no Roman losses. In Rome, Cato proposed handing Caesar over to the Germans for violating a truce (Plutarch, Caesar 22). Nico Roymans identified the site with Kessel, at the confluence of the Meuse and the Waal, where human remains, weapons and objects from the 1st century BC have been found, and considers it a case of genocidal slaughter; Caesar's figure, on the other hand, has no independent support.

hechos/puente-sobre-el-rin/resumen.texto: Caesar had a wooden bridge built across the Rhine in ten days, probably near Neuwied or Koblenz, spent eighteen days on German territory to intimidate the Suebi, and destroyed it on his return (BG IV.16-19); in 53 BC he built another. His technical description (IV.17) is one of the most detailed accounts of a Roman military engineering work. The Rhine stood in his Commentaries as the border between Gauls and Germans, a division that modern historians see in part as a political construction of Caesar's.

hechos/rebelion-de-ambiorix/resumen.texto: In the winter of 54 BC, with the legions dispersed because of the grain shortage, the Eburones of Ambiorix and Catuvolcus convinced the legates Sabinus and Cotta to leave the camp at Atuatuca, and destroyed a legion and five cohorts in an ambush (BG V.24-37).
