The Nervii then besieged the camp of Quintus Cicero, which held out until Caesar arrived (V.38-52), and the Treveri of Indutiomarus attacked Labienus. It was Caesar's worst defeat in Gaul, which he attributes to Sabinus' recklessness.

hechos/devastacion-del-pais-eburon/titul.texto: Caesar devastates the land of the Eburones

hechos/devastacion-del-pais-eburon/resum.texto: To avenge Atuatuca, Caesar invaded the territory of the Eburones and invited the neighboring peoples to plunder it, so that the name of that people would be destroyed without risking his soldiers (BG VI.34-35); in 51 BC he devastated it again (Hirtius, BG VIII.24-25). Ambiorix was never caught. Roymans (2019) links to these campaigns the population decline shown by archaeology in the south of the Netherlands and Belgium, and Raaflaub (2021) discusses them among the episodes that could fit the modern definition of genocide, because Caesar himself declares the purpose of erasing the name of that people. Roymans and Fernández-Götz do not speak of total extermination but of a sharp fall in population.

hechos/ejecucion-de-acco/resumen.texto: At an assembly of Gaul held at Durocortorum (Reims), Caesar tried the conspiracy of the Senones and Carnutes and sentenced their leader Acco to die “according to the custom of their ancestors,” by flogging and beheading (BG VI.44). The following year, the Gauls preparing the general revolt recalled his death as proof of what awaited them (BG VII.1).

hechos/masacre-de-cenabo/titulo.texto: Massacre of Roman traders at Cenabum

hechos/masacre-de-cenabo/resumen.texto: At the beginning of 52 BC, taking advantage of the crisis in Rome after Clodius' murder, the Carnutes of Gutruatus and Conconnetodumnus killed the Roman traders settled at Cenabum (Orléans), among them an equestrian in charge of the grain supply; the news, shouted across the fields, reached the Arvernian country in a single day (BG VII.1-3). Caesar took and burned Cenabum a few weeks later and gave the city and its people to plunder (VII.11).

hechos/proclamacion-de-vercingetorix/res.texto: The young Arvernian noble Vercingetorix, expelled from Gergovia by his uncle Gobannitio and by the nobles who feared a war, gathered “the poor and the desperate,” returned, proclaimed himself king, and won the support of almost all the peoples of central and western Gaul (BG VII.4). Caesar describes his severe discipline, with punishments by fire and mutilation, and his decision to burn villages and granaries to leave the Roman army without supplies (VII.4, VII.14).

hechos/sitio-de-avarico/resumen.texto: The Bituriges begged Vercingetorix not to burn Avaricum, and Caesar besieged it for almost a month with earthworks and towers against the wall of timber and stone that he himself describes as the “Gallic wall” (BG VII.13-28). When he took it, his soldiers spared neither the old, nor women, nor children: Caesar says that of some 40,000 inhabitants only 800 reached Vercingetorix (VII.28).

hechos/batalla-de-gergovia/resumen.texto: Caesar besieged the Arvernian oppidum of Gergovia and launched an assault that his soldiers carried further than ordered, up to the walls, where they were repulsed, with 46 centurions and almost seven hundred soldiers dead (BG VII.36-53). It was Caesar's only defeat against Vercingetorix; he attributes it to the indiscipline of his troops. Shortly afterward the Aedui, his main allies, joined the revolt.

hechos/batalla-de-lutecia/resumen.texto: While Caesar was at Gergovia, his legate Labienus marched against the Parisii and their neighbors, crossed the Seine by surprise and defeated the army of the Aulercan Camulogenus, who died in the fighting (BG VII.57-62). It is the first well-documented event in the history of Paris.

hechos/concilio-de-bibracte/titulo.texto: The assembly at Bibracte confirms Vercingetorix

hechos/concilio-de-bibracte/resumen.texto: After the defection of the Aedui, an assembly of all of Gaul held at Bibracte unanimously voted Vercingetorix supreme commander; the Aedui, who aspired to the command, accepted him reluctantly (BG VII.63). The Remi and the Lingones, allies of Rome, did not attend, nor did the Treveri. It is the moment of greatest political unity in Gaul recorded in the sources.

hechos/batalla-del-vingeanne/resumen.texto: The Gallic cavalry attacked Caesar's army on its march toward the Province and was defeated by the German horsemen in Roman service, with the capture of three Aeduan leaders (BG VII.66-67). Vercingetorix withdrew to Alesia, which allowed Caesar to besiege him. The exact site, near the Vingeanne river according to the most accepted hypothesis, is disputed.

hechos/sitio-de-alesia/resumen.texto: Caesar surrounded the oppidum of Alesia, where Vercingetorix had shut himself in with 80,000 men, with a double line of fortifications some 16 and 21 kilometers long, facing both the besieged and the relief army, which Caesar says numbered 8,000 horsemen and 250,000 infantry (BG VII.68-90). The Mandubii expelled their women and children from the town, and Caesar did not let them pass (VII.78); Cassius Dio (XL.40) tells that they died between the lines. The final attack, led by Vercassivellaunus, failed and Gaul surrendered. The Franco-German excavations of 1991-1997 confirmed the Roman lines on Mont Auxois. The figures for the relief army, larger than those of any battle of the period known, have been considered greatly exaggerated in modern historiography since Hans Delbrück (1900).

hechos/rendicion-de-vercingetorix/resume.texto: Caesar only says that Vercingetorix was handed over and the weapons thrown down, and that he gave each soldier a prisoner as booty, except the Aedui and Arverni, whom he freed to win back their loyalty (BG VII.89-90). Plutarch (Caesar 27), Florus (I.45) and Cassius Dio (XL.41) tell that he rode up in his best armor, circled Caesar, threw down his weapons and sat silently at his feet. The scene, written a century and a half later, is the one that French painting and academic art made canonical.

hechos/campana-contra-los-belovacos/resu.texto: In 51 BC the Bellovaci, led by Correus and the Atrebatan Commius, resisted Caesar in a fortified camp and set ambushes for him; Correus died fighting and the Bellovaci surrendered (Hirtius, BG VIII.6-23). Hirtius says that Labienus tried to have Commius murdered during a meeting.

hechos/sitio-de-uxeloduno/resumen.texto: The last rebels, led by the Cadurcian Lucterius and the Senonian Drappes, held out in the oppidum of Uxellodunum until the Romans diverted by a gallery the spring that supplied them (Hirtius, BG VIII.32-44). Caesar had the hands cut off of all who had carried weapons and let them live as a warning, according to Hirtius, who presents it as proof of his usual clemency. Excavations at the Puy d'Issolud found the gallery.

hechos/ejecucion-de-vercingetorix/resume.texto: After six years in prison, Vercingetorix was paraded in Caesar's triumph over Gaul in 46 BC and executed, as was customary with defeated leaders (Cassius Dio XL.41, XLIII.19). Caesar does not mention his end in the Commentaries, which finish in 52 BC.

hechos/fundacion-de-lugdunum/resumen.texto: Lucius Munatius Plancus founded a Roman colony at the confluence of the Rhône and the Saône, on a site whose Gaulish name, Lugudunon, is usually translated as “fortress of Lugus” (Cassius Dio XLVI.50). It became the capital of the three provinces of Gallia Comata and the seat of its federal sanctuary.

hechos/organizacion-de-las-tres-galias/r.texto: In 27 BC Augustus convened an assembly at Narbo, carried out the first census of Gaul and divided it, apart from Narbonensis, into three provinces: Aquitania, Lugdunensis and Belgica (Cassius Dio LIII.22; Strabo IV.1.1). The ancient Gaulish peoples became “cities” (civitates) with their capitals, many of them new. There were revolts in Aquitania and among the Treveri and Morini in those same years.

hechos/revuelta-de-floro-y-sacroviro/res.texto: The Gallic nobles Julius Florus, a Treveran, and Julius Sacrovir, an Aeduan, both Roman citizens, roused the cities burdened with debts from loans and taxes. Sacrovir took Augustodunum with the young nobles who studied there and armed gladiators in armor, but he was defeated by Gaius Silius and committed suicide, as did Florus (Tacitus, Annals III.40-47). Tacitus says that almost all the cities of Gaul were involved; the Treveran Julius Indus helped suppress it. It was the first great revolt of Romanized Gaul, led by aristocrats already integrated into Rome.

hechos/discurso-de-claudio-sobre-los-gal.texto: Claudius asks the Senate to admit Gallic nobles

Responding to the petition of the notables of Gallia Comata to hold magistracies in Rome, Emperor Claudius, born in Lugdunum, argued in the Senate that Rome had always grown by incorporating foreigners, from the Etruscan kings to the senators of Vienne, and recalled that Gaul had a hundred years of loyalty. The Senate granted the right first to the Aedui (Tacitus, Annals XI.23-25). The text of the speech survives on the Claudian Tablet of Lyon, and its comparison with Tacitus' version shows how ancient historians rewrote the speeches they quoted.

hechos/rebelion-de-vindex/resumen.texto: Gaius Julius Vindex, governor of Lugdunensis and a noble of Aquitanian origin, rose against Nero in March 68 with the support of the Aedui, Sequani and Arverni, and offered the empire to Galba. The Rhine legions, who did not accept him, defeated him near Vesontio with thousands of Gauls dead, and he committed suicide (Cassius Dio LXIII.22-25; Plutarch, Galba 4-6). Nero's fall came weeks later. Since Peter Brunt (1959) most historians have seen in it a revolt of senators against Nero rather than a national Gallic uprising, as it was read in the 19th century; others point out that his troops were Gallic and that the Treveri and Lingones saw it as a matter for their rivals.

hechos/revuelta-de-marico/resumen.texto: In the middle of the civil war, a Boian named Maricus proclaimed himself a god and “liberator of the Gauls,” gathered eight thousand followers in the country of the Aedui and was defeated by the Aeduan militia; they threw him to the beasts and then executed him before Vitellius (Tacitus, Histories II.61). Tacitus treats him with contempt; some historians read him as a peasant movement with a religious, millenarian tone.

hechos/rebelion-de-los-batavos/resumen.texto: The Batavian prince Julius Civilis raised his people and the German auxiliary troops on the Rhine, besieged the camp at Vetera, and won over the Treveri and Lingones (Tacitus, Histories IV-V). It was suppressed by Quintus Petillius Cerialis in 70, after several battles. Tacitus, the only source, breaks off the account when Civilis negotiates with Cerialis.

hechos/imperio-de-las-galias-70/resumen.texto: At the beginning of 70, the Treveran Julius Classicus and Julius Tutor and the Lingonian Julius Sabinus, Gallo-Roman officers and nobles, proclaimed an “Empire of the Gauls” allied with Civilis, and made the defeated Rhine legions swear loyalty (Tacitus, Histories IV.54-79). Tacitus says that the burning of the Capitol in 69 had led the druids to believe that dominion was passing to the northern peoples. An assembly of the Gallic cities held at Durocortorum (Reims) preferred peace with Rome (IV.68-69), and Petillius Cerialis defeated the rebels at Rigodunum and Trier. Tacitus attributes to him a speech according to which in Gaul there had always been kings and wars until it accepted Roman laws (IV.73-74). Historians see it as an attempt by part of the northeastern aristocracy, not as a movement of all of Gaul.

hechos/ulpiano-admite-el-galo/titulo.texto: Ulpian admits wills in the Gaulish language

hechos/ulpiano-admite-el-galo/resumen.texto: The jurist Ulpian, praetorian prefect under Severus Alexander, wrote that fideicommissa (requests left in a will) could be made in any language, “not only in Latin or Greek, but also in Punic, in Gaulish or in that of any other people.” The passage is preserved in Justinian's Digest (XXXII.11). Because it appears next to Punic, it is generally read as referring to Gaulish and not to the Latin of Gaul, and it is one of the indications that at the beginning of the 3rd century there were people who dictated their wishes in Gaulish. It is a general rule and does not say how many spoke it.

hechos/martires-de-lyon/resumen.texto: In 177 the population of Lugdunum attacked the Christians of the city, largely Greek immigrants from Asia, and the authorities tortured and executed several dozen, among them Bishop Pothinus and the slave Blandina. The letter from the churches of Lyon and Vienne that tells this survives in Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History V.1-3). Irenaeus, who succeeded Pothinus, wrote soon after that he lived among the Celts and used a barbarian language.

hechos/destruccion-del-vasso-galatae/tit.texto: Destruction of the temple of Vasso Galatae

hechos/destruccion-del-vasso-galatae/res.texto: Gregory of Tours (History of the Franks I.32) tells that the Alamannic king Chrocus destroyed, in Clermont, in the time of Valerian and Gallienus, a temple with walls of marble and mosaic “which in the Gaulish language they call Vasso Galatae.” It is one of the last Gaulish names cited as such by a Latin author, at the end of the 6th century. Many linguists take it as evidence that Gaulish was still spoken in Auvergne, and others warn that Gregory may have been repeating a traditional name. It is disputed whether the temple was that of Mercury on the Puy de Dôme or another in the city, and the date of Chrocus' raid, which some historians put in the 5th century.

hechos/imperio-galo/resumen.texto: In 260 the general Postumus proclaimed himself emperor in Gaul and ruled, from Cologne and Trier, Gaul, Britain and for a time Hispania, with his own consuls and coinage. His successors lasted until Tetricus surrendered to Aurelian in 274. It was not a movement of the Gauls against Rome but a regional Roman empire born from the crisis of the 3rd century, although 19th-century historians read it as Gaulish nationalism. The sources are brief (Aurelius Victor, Eutropius, the unreliable Historia Augusta), and the coinage is the main documentary source.

hechos/bagaudas/resumen.texto: The Bagaudae were bands of peasants, coloni and deserters who rose up in Gaul and Hispania in 284-286, suppressed by Maximian, and again in the 5th century, above all in Armorica, where Tibatto led them in 435-437. Salvian of Marseilles (On the Governance of God V) presents them as people driven to rebellion by taxes and injustice. Edward A. Thompson (1952) interpreted them as a class revolt of peasants against landowners; others, such as John Drinkwater, see in them rather regional self-defense groups led by local notables, and the old reading that made them a “Celtic” resistance has no support in the sources. Their name may come from a Gaulish word for “fighters.”

hechos/aparicion-de-los-oppida/resumen.texto: From the middle of the 2nd century BC large fortified settlements were founded in Gaul and central Europe, which Caesar calls oppida (Bibracte, Gergovia, Alesia, Avaricum, Manching). They had earthen, timber and stone walls, like the “Gallic wall” he describes in BG VII.23, quarters of artisans, sanctuaries, assembly squares and minting workshops. Stephan Fichtl (2000) interprets them as political capitals of the Gaulish “cities,” often founded all at once and not grown from villages; other archaeologists debate how much they were cities and how much refuges or ceremonial centers. They contradict the image of the Gaul living in villages without walls that Polybius (II.17) transmits for the Gauls of Italy.

hechos/vino-por-esclavos/titulo.texto: Italian wine in exchange for slaves

hechos/vino-por-esclavos/resumen.texto: Diodorus (V.26.3), following Posidonius, says that the Gauls were so fond of wine that Italian merchants traded an amphora for a slave. Italian amphorae of the Dressel 1 type appear by the thousands in the oppida and rivers of Gaul between the middle of the 2nd century and the middle of the 1st century BC, in places such as Bibracte, Corent, Chalon-sur-Saône or Toulouse. André Tchernia (1983) linked the volume of that trade to Italy's demand for slaves; Matthieu Poux (2004) emphasized the use of wine in the banquets and rituals of the Gaulish aristocracy, and other authors warn that Diodorus' phrase is also a commonplace about the drunken barbarian. The exact equivalence “one amphora, one slave” cannot be verified.

hechos/sociedad-gala-segun-cesar/resumen.texto: Caesar (BG VI.11-20) describes a Gaul divided into factions in every people, village and household, where only the druids and the “knights” (equites) count, who have clients and retainers (ambacts), while the commoners, in debt, live almost like slaves. He says that husbands have the right of life and death over wives and children, and that husband and wife bring equal goods to the marriage. Other passages show assemblies, senates such as that of the Nervii, and annual magistrates such as the vergobret of the Aedui (BG I.16, VII.32-33). It is a text written in the middle of the war, which takes commonplaces from Posidonius and simplifies them for Roman readers. The archaeology of the oppida, the coins, inscriptions and workshops show a more complex society, with specialized artisans, long-distance trade and elites who imitated Mediterranean ways of life. Caesar's figures and categories do not allow us to know how many people were free or dependent.

hechos/colonias-de-masalia/titulo.texto: Massalia founds colonies on the Gaulish coast

hechos/colonias-de-masalia/resumen.texto: Massalia, founded by the Phocaeans around 600 BC, created between the 5th and 3rd centuries BC a network of colonies and posts along the coast, from Agathe (Agde) to Nicaea (Nice) and Antipolis (Antibes), and others in Hispania such as Emporion. Strabo (IV.1.5) says that the Gauls learned from it to write their contracts in Greek, and Justin (XLIII.4) that it taught them to cultivate the vine and the olive and to surround their cities with walls, a praise of Greek “civilization” that also reflects the viewpoint of Pompeius Trogus, a Romanized Gaul. Relations with the Ligurians and the Salluvii of the interior alternated between trade and war.

hechos/legion-de-las-alondras/titulo.texto: Caesar recruits a legion of Gauls

hechos/legion-de-las-alondras/resumen.texto: Caesar recruited, from among the Gauls of the Province, who were not citizens, a legion which he equipped and trained in the Roman way, and to which he granted citizenship. Suetonius (Caesar 24) says it was called by a Gaulish word, Alauda (“lark”), which Pliny (XI.121) links to the crests of the helmets. It was the first legion formed with non-citizens, and it shows how the conquest incorporated the Gauls into the Roman army; Gallic and German cavalry was also decisive in his campaigns.

hechos/romanizacion-de-la-galia/resumen.texto: In the two centuries after the conquest, Gaul filled with cities with forums, temples and theaters, villas, roads and workshops. The elites took Roman names, citizenship and offices, Latin became the language of writing, and Gaulish gods were worshipped with Roman-style names and temples, while Gaulish continued to be spoken and written in the countryside and in workshops. Strabo (IV.1.12) already said that the Cavari of Narbonensis were Roman in language and customs. The word “Romanization” is debated: Greg Woolf (1998) describes a cultural change sought by local elites, and others, such as Jane Webster, prefer to speak of mixing or “creolization” and of resistance among the popular classes. The old thesis of a Celtic culture that survived intact beneath the Roman surface is not supported by the sources.

hechos/batalla-de-cavillono/titulo.texto: Cavalry Engagement after the Arar (Saône) (Battle of Cavillonum)

hechos/batalla-de-cavillono/resumen.texto: The day after the battle of the Arar, Caesar sent his cavalry, about 4,000 horsemen from the Province and allied Aedui, to watch the enemy; they advanced too far, and 500 Helvetian horsemen charged them on bad ground. The Aedui of Dumnorix were the first to flee (I.18), and the Romans withdrew with few losses (Gallic War I.15 and I.18); Caesar followed the Helvetii for about fifteen more days. Caesar does not give the name of the place: “Cavillonum” (Chalon-sur-Saône) is the location proposed by Wikipedia, and it is only approximate.

hechos/batalla-de-octoduro/resumen.texto: In the winter of 57–56 BC Caesar sent Servius Sulpicius Galba with the Twelfth Legion to secure the passage over the Great St Bernard, where Roman merchants suffered attacks and tolls from the Nantuates, Veragri and Seduni. Galba wintered at Octodurus (Martigny, Valais), and within a few days the tribes, who according to Caesar feared a lasting occupation, wanted to recover their hostages and scorned a small legion, so they attacked from the heights. After about six hours of defense, the Romans made a sortie and, according to Caesar (Gallic War III.1–6), killed a third of some 30,000 attackers, a figure considered inflated. Short of supplies, Galba burned the village and withdrew to the land of the Allobroges. Caesar presents this as a victory, and some historians see the withdrawal as a setback.

lugares/bibracte/resumen.texto: Oppidum of the Aedui on Mont Beuvray, of some two hundred hectares within its outer wall, with artisan quarters, Roman-style houses and thousands of Italian wine amphorae. There an assembly of Gaul confirmed Vercingetorix as leader in 52 BC, and Caesar spent the following winter at Bibracte (BG VII.63, VII.90); it is generally assumed that he wrote part of his Commentaries there. It was abandoned around the turn of the era in favor of Augustodunum (Autun). It was excavated by Jacques-Gabriel Bulliot (1867-1895) and his nephew Joseph Déchelette (1897-1907), and since the late 20th century it has been the seat of a European research program.

lugares/gergovia/resumen.texto: Oppidum of the Arverni on a plateau south of Clermont-Ferrand, where Vercingetorix repulsed Caesar's assault in 52 BC (BG VII.36-53). Excavations found the two Roman camps and the ditch that linked them, as Caesar describes; the Gaulish occupation of the plateau seems to have been concentrated in the decades of the conquest, and Corent and Gondole, in the same area, were earlier or contemporary Arvernian centers. It was abandoned in the time of Augustus in favor of Augustonemetum.

lugares/alesia/resumen.texto: Oppidum of the Mandubii on Mont Auxois, at Alise-Sainte-Reine, where Caesar besieged Vercingetorix in 52 BC. Excavations by Napoleon III (1861-1865) and the Franco-German excavations of Michel Reddé and Siegmar von Schnurbein (1991-1997) found the Roman siege lines, and a Gaulish inscription of the 1st century names the place as Alisiia. The alternative location at Chaux-des-Crotenay, proposed by André Berthier in 1962, is not accepted by academic archaeology. After the conquest it became a Gallo-Roman town.

lugares/uxeloduno/resumen.texto: Cadurcian oppidum where the last rebels held out in 51 BC, until Caesar cut off their water. Excavations by Jean-Pierre Girault at Puy d'Issolud (Vayrac), between 1993 and 2001, found the Roman gallery that diverted the spring and hundreds of arrowheads, and the French Ministry of Culture accepted the identification.

lugares/avarico/resumen.texto: Capital of the Bituriges Cubi, already a princely center in the 5th century BC, which Caesar considered “almost the most beautiful city in all of Gaul” (BG VII.15). In 52 BC the Bituriges asked that it not be burned as part of Vercingetorix's scorched-earth tactic, and Caesar took it after a siege of almost a month. It is present-day Bourges.

lugares/entremont/resumen.texto: Oppidum of the Salluvii (or Saluvii), north of Aix-en-Provence, with a wall with towers, stone houses in regular blocks, and a portico with pillars of carved skulls and statues of seated warriors. The Romans destroyed it around 123 BC, in the war that followed Massalia's request for help, and founded Aquae Sextiae at its foot; it had a brief later occupation.

lugares/enserune/resumen.texto: Oppidum between Béziers and Narbo, occupied from the 6th century BC to the 1st century, with silos, stone houses and a cremation necropolis with Greek and Etruscan vessels. It has inscriptions in Iberian script and Celtic objects of La Tène type, which is why it is studied as a mixed site between the Iberian, Gaulish and Greek worlds.

lugares/corent/resumen.texto: Plateau in Arvernian country where excavations led by Matthieu Poux since 2001 found a sanctuary, an assembly building, markets, workshops and enormous quantities of Italian wine amphorae of the 2nd and 1st centuries BC. Poux interprets it as a political center of the Arverni prior to Gergovia, perhaps their capital, a reading that other archaeologists dispute.

lugares/narbona/resumen.texto: The first Roman colony outside Italy in Gaul, founded around 118 BC next to an indigenous settlement on the Via Domitia. It gave its name to the province of Narbonensis and was its capital; Cicero called it “watchtower and bulwark of the Roman people” (Pro Fonteio 13).

lugares/vienne-galia/resumen.texto: Main center of the Allobroges on the Rhône, subjected to Rome in 121 BC, which became a Roman colony and one of the richest cities of Narbonensis. In 48 Claudius held it up as an example of a province that provided senators (Claudian Tablet).

lugares/autun/resumen.texto: City founded in the time of Augustus as the new capital of the Aedui, replacing Bibracte. Tacitus (Annals III.43) says that in 21 the sons of the Gaulish nobility studied there, and Julius Sacrovir took them as hostages; at the end of the 3rd century its schools were still famous.

lugares/titelberg/resumen.texto: Oppidum of the Treveri in southern Luxembourg, with a large public square enclosed by a ditch, coin-minting workshops and artisan houses. It remained inhabited as a settlement in Roman times.

lugares/glanum/resumen.texto: Salluvian settlement next to a sacred spring, near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, which in the 2nd century BC adopted buildings in the Greek style through its contact with Massalia and later became a Roman town. It has Gaulish inscriptions in the Greek alphabet. It was abandoned around 260, after the raids of the Alamanni.

lugares/lattara/resumen.texto: Port on a lagoon near Montpellier, founded around 500 BC and frequented by Etruscan and then Massaliote merchants. Excavations, since 1983, show the shift from Etruscan to Greek amphorae and then to Italian ones. It is one of the keys to understanding Mediterranean trade with the Gauls.

lugares/la-graufesenque/resumen.texto: Major pottery center of Condatomagus, near Millau, which in the 1st century exported sigillata ware to the whole Roman West, especially to the Rhine frontier. At the site, dozens of plates were found with records of kiln firings written in Gaulish in Latin cursive script, which show potters using their language at work.
